title: Unjust Laws
objective: After this level you can explain how laws can be unjust and how they get repealed.
summary: Thinkers disagree about what to do with a law you believe is unjust. Thoreau and King argued for civil disobedience; Plato's Socrates chose to obey. The legal route out of a law is repeal.

cards.headline: In 1846, a writer spent a night in jail rather than pay a tax.
cards.body: Henry David Thoreau refused to pay his poll tax in Concord, Massachusetts, in protest against slavery and the Mexican-American War. His night in a cell opens a long argument: what should you do about a law you believe is unjust? Thinkers have given very different answers.

cards.headline: Thoreau: don't be the tool
cards.body: Thoreau turned the experience into an essay, "Resistance to Civil Government" (1849), later known as "Civil Disobedience." If a law requires you to be "the agent of injustice to another," he wrote, "then, I say, break the law." The essay went on to influence Gandhi and Martin Luther King Jr.

cards.headline: King: break it openly
cards.body: In his Letter from Birmingham Jail (1963), King argued that people have a moral responsibility to obey just laws and to disobey unjust ones. But not in secret: one who breaks an unjust law, he wrote, must do so "openly, lovingly, and with a willingness to accept the penalty." He'd been arrested for parading without a permit. A permit rule is fine in itself, he argued; it becomes unjust when used to maintain segregation.

cards.headline: Socrates: stay and obey
cards.body: In Plato's Crito, Socrates makes the opposite choice. Awaiting execution, he refuses a chance to escape, though he thinks his sentence unjust. By living in Athens all his life, he argues, he had implicitly agreed to obey its laws. Sound like Level 7's social contract? It's the same idea, told as a prison conversation.

cards.fact: South Africa's parliament repealed its race-classification law in 1991.
cards.context: The Population Registration Act of 1950 had classified all South Africans by race. It ended through the lawmaking process you've followed all chapter: a new act repealed it.

objective: After this level you can compare the main legal traditions of the world.
summary: Civil law starts from written codes descended from Roman law; common law builds on precedent. Customary and Muslim law and mixed systems, like bijural Canada, complete the map.

cards.headline: Move from Ottawa to Montreal, and your contracts switch legal families.
cards.body: Canada is bijural. In Quebec, private law follows the civil law tradition, set out mainly in the Civil Code of Quebec. The rest of Canada uses common law. Same country, two ways of thinking about law. What's the difference?

cards.headline: Civil law: start with the code
cards.body: Civil law, the tradition of continental Europe, traces back to Roman law as compiled under Emperor Justinian. Its heart is a comprehensive written code. France's Napoleonic Code of 1804 became a model for many nations. Today civil law runs across continental Europe, much of Latin America, and parts of Asia and Africa. Like Hammurabi's stone from Level 4, the law starts as a written text.

mascot.line: Careful: "civil law" here is a legal tradition. Level 56's civil cases are something else.

cards.headline: Common law: start with the cases
cards.body: Common law grew up in medieval England from judges' decisions, recorded in reports of decided cases. Judges follow earlier decisions, called precedent, so similar cases are decided alike. It's the basis of law in the United States and most Commonwealth countries. In civil law, you open the code. In common law, you open the case reports.

cards.headline: Custom, religion and mixtures
cards.body: JuriGlobe, a University of Ottawa project, sorts the world's legal systems into five categories: civil law, common law, customary law, Muslim law and mixed systems. Most Muslim-majority countries use Western-style criminal codes but keep sharia mainly for family law, such as marriage, divorce and inheritance; Turkey replaced it with secular codes. And mixtures are common: South Africa and Scotland blend civil and common law, while Ghana and Kenya blend common and customary law.

title: Courts
objective: After this level you can explain what courts do.
summary: Courts settle disputes without force: they find the facts and apply the law. Valencia's Water Tribunal has done it at a cathedral door since al-Andalus.

cards.headline: Every Thursday at noon, a court meets on a cathedral doorstep.
cards.body: In Valencia, Spain, eight judges in farmers' blouses gather at the cathedral door to settle quarrels over irrigation water. The farmers who come before them elect them. The tribunal goes back to al-Andalus, between the 9th and 13th centuries, and UNESCO listed it as world heritage in 2009. Why do people keep bringing their fights to it? Because that is exactly what a court is for.

cards.headline: A referee instead of a fist
cards.body: Picture two farmers, one canal and a dry summer. Without a court, Britannica notes, people settle disputes by force. A court is a person or body with the authority to hear and resolve disputes, and its first job is keeping the peace as an impartial, authoritative judge. Remember Level 1's Sumer, where sharing river water needed a central authority? Valencia's farmers found theirs on a church step.

cards.headline: Two questions, in order
cards.body: Every trial court answers two questions: what happened, and what does the law say about it? It works out the facts, then applies the law to them. Did the farmer open his gate out of turn? That's a fact. What follows when someone does? That's law, Level 4's rule backed by authority. In Valencia it all happens out loud, in Valencian, with the verdict given on the spot. No paperwork required, and no time to lose your temper.

mascot.line: Nobody judges their own case. Hold on to that; the next level builds on it.

cards.fact: The judge from the farmers' own canal has to sit out.
cards.context: To keep the Water Tribunal impartial, the syndic of the canal the disputing farmers belong to takes no part in the deliberation. And there's no appeal: the sentence is final. Most court systems add a second layer instead, appeal courts, whose job is to check whether the trial court applied the law correctly.

title: Judges
objective: After this level you can explain what judges do and why their independence matters.
summary: Judges keep trials fair, rule on the law and pass sentence. After James II replaced judges, the Act of Settlement (1701) made their jobs safe; the UN's 1985 principles went global.

cards.headline: In 1686, a king replaced judges until he got the ruling he wanted.
cards.body: James II of England wanted the power to excuse people from the Test Oath, which holders of public office had to take. After a number of judges had been replaced, the court in Godden v Hales found in the king's favour. The judges' names changed; the answer changed with them. That's the problem this level is about.

cards.headline: The referee, not a player
cards.body: What does a judge actually do? In an English Crown Court trial, the judge makes sure the trial is fair, resolves the legal questions, directs the jury on the law and, if there's a conviction, imposes the sentence. The judge doesn't take a side. A referee who is secretly on one team isn't a referee; he's a very well-dressed player.

cards.headline: 1701: the job becomes safe
cards.body: England's answer came in the Act of Settlement of 1701. Senior judges would now hold office during good behaviour, not at the monarch's pleasure, and only both Houses of Parliament together could remove them. Their salaries had to be fixed too, so nobody could squeeze them with money. A judge who can't be fired for the wrong answer can afford to give the right one.

cards.fact: Independent judges are now a worldwide standard.
cards.context: The UN's 1985 Basic Principles on the Independence of the Judiciary say judges must decide impartially, on the facts and the law, free of improper pressures or threats from anyone. It's Level 51's Water Tribunal rule, scaled up: there, the syndic of the disputing farmers' canal sits out, so nobody judges their own case.

title: Juries
objective: After this level you can explain how juries work.
summary: Juries of ordinary citizens, picked at random, decide guilt while the judge handles the law. Bushel's Case (1670) ruled jurors can't be punished for their verdict; Japan mixes citizens and judges.

cards.headline: In 1670, a London jury was locked up without food for saying "not guilty".
cards.body: The defendants were two Quakers, William Penn and William Mead, charged over preaching. The jurors acquitted them anyway. They were held without food, then fined and jailed for their verdict. One juror, Edward Bushel, refused to accept that. What he won still matters to every jury today.

cards.headline: Twelve people you've never met
cards.body: Here's how it works in England and Wales today. In a Crown Court trial, a jury of 12 members of the public decides whether the defendant is guilty. They're chosen at random from the electoral register; nobody volunteers. The judge handles the law, directs the jury and passes sentence. It's a lottery nobody enters on purpose.

cards.headline: Bushel's Case: the verdict is the jury's
cards.body: Bushel challenged his imprisonment, and in 1670 Chief Justice John Vaughan agreed with him: jurors cannot be punished for their verdict. The court judges the law; the jury judges the facts. Why does it matter? If jurors can be jailed for the wrong answer, the jury is just the judge with twelve extra chairs.

title: Innocent Until Proven Guilty
objective: After this level you can explain the presumption of innocence.
summary: The accused doesn't have to prove innocence: the prosecution must prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt. Woolmington v DPP (1935) called it the golden thread; the UDHR made it a human right.

cards.headline: In 1935, a conviction fell because the judge put the burden on the wrong side.
cards.body: Reginald Woolmington said the gun that killed his wife went off by accident. His trial judge told the jury that, once the killing was proved, it was up to Woolmington to prove it was an accident. The House of Lords quashed his conviction. Not because anyone proved him innocent, but because nobody should have had to.

mascot.line: Innocent until proven guilty isn't a guess about anyone. It's a rule about who has to do the proving.

cards.headline: The golden thread
cards.body: Viscount Sankey's judgment gave the principle its famous name. Running through the web of English criminal law, he said, is one golden thread: it is the duty of the prosecution to prove the prisoner's guilt. The accused doesn't have to prove anything. Accusing is the easy part; proving is the prosecution's job.

cards.headline: Beyond reasonable doubt
cards.body: How sure must a jury be? In criminal cases, the prosecution has to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt; if a reasonable doubt remains, the accused goes free. The system is tilted on purpose. In the 1760s William Blackstone put it in one line: it is better that ten guilty persons escape than that one innocent suffer.

cards.fact: It's written into the Universal Declaration of Human Rights.
cards.context: Article 11 of the 1948 Declaration says everyone charged with a penal offence has the right to be presumed innocent until proved guilty. The golden thread of an English courtroom is also a promise made to the whole world.

title: Lawyers
objective: After this level you can explain what lawyers do on each side of a case.
summary: A prosecutor brings the case for the state; a defence lawyer tests it. England's cab-rank rule keeps lawyers open to all; Gideon v Wainwright (1963) gave poor U.S. defendants a lawyer.

cards.headline: A prisoner's handwritten petition changed who gets a lawyer.
cards.body: In 1961 Clarence Earl Gideon was charged with breaking into a Florida pool hall. He couldn't afford a lawyer and asked the judge for one. Florida only appointed lawyers in capital cases, so Gideon defended himself, and lost. From prison he sent the Supreme Court a handwritten petition.

cards.headline: Two sides, two jobs
cards.body: A criminal trial has a lawyer on each side. The prosecutor brings the case for the state. In England and Wales that's the Crown Prosecution Service, independent of the police, which decides which police-investigated cases go to court and then prosecutes them. The defence lawyer represents the accused and tests every piece of evidence. Level 54's golden thread needs someone to pull on it.

cards.headline: The cab-rank rule
cards.body: How can a lawyer defend someone accused of something terrible? In England, barristers follow the cab-rank rule: like a taxi at the front of the rank, they must generally take a suitable case whatever they think of the client or the cause. The point, says the Bar Standards Board, is that everyone can get legal representation. Defending someone isn't endorsing them. It's making sure the case gets tested.

cards.fact: Same man, same charge, different result.
cards.context: In 1963 the Supreme Court ruled unanimously that states must provide a lawyer to defendants in felony cases who can't afford one. Gideon got a retrial, this time with a lawyer, who discredited the prosecution's key witness. The jury acquitted him. The big difference was the person standing next to him.

title: Criminal and Civil Law
objective: After this level you can compare criminal and civil cases.
summary: Criminal cases are brought by the state and can end in punishment; civil cases settle disputes between people or organisations, usually with damages, and need only 'more likely than not'.

cards.headline: Acquitted in 1995. Found liable in 1997. Same man, same two deaths.
cards.body: In 1995 a jury acquitted O.J. Simpson of murdering Nicole Brown Simpson and Ronald Goldman. In 1997 a different jury, in a civil trial, found him liable for their deaths and ordered him to pay $33.5 million in damages to the families. A contradiction? No. Two different kinds of case, asking two different questions.

cards.headline: Criminal: the state brings the case
cards.body: A criminal case is about an alleged crime. It comes to court when the state decides to prosecute; in England and Wales that decision is usually the Crown Prosecution Service's. If the accused is convicted, the sentence can be prison, community punishment or a fine. The victim isn't suing anyone. The state is the one asking for punishment.

cards.headline: Civil: people versus people
cards.body: A civil case is a dispute between people, businesses or organisations: damaged goods, say, or an unpaid debt. Nobody goes to prison for losing. The winner may get damages, meaning money, or a court order telling someone to do or stop doing something. It's less "you broke the law" and more "you owe me".

mascot.line: Criminal and civil get mixed up. The quickest tell is the bar: reasonable doubt, or more likely than not.

cards.headline: Two different bars
cards.body: Here's the key. Criminal guilt must be proved beyond reasonable doubt. A civil claim needs only to be more likely than not: the balance of probabilities, anything over 50%. So a jury can have a reasonable doubt that Simpson committed murder, while another decides it's more likely than not he was responsible. Same facts, two bars, two answers.

title: Supreme Courts
objective: After this level you can explain courts that decide what a constitution means.
summary: Judicial review lets courts void unconstitutional laws: any U.S. court since Marbury v Madison (1803), special courts like Germany's. UK courts can only declare a law incompatible.

cards.headline: In 2024, Germany's top constitutional court received 4,640 new cases.
cards.body: About 96% were constitutional complaints. Any person in Germany can lodge one, claiming that a public authority has violated their fundamental rights, and about two-thirds of the 2024 complaints came without a lawyer. Fewer than 2 in 100 succeed. But when one does, the court can declare a law void. How can a court overrule a law?

cards.headline: Judicial review
cards.body: A constitution is the rulebook for the people who make the rules. Judicial review is the power of courts to examine laws and government actions and declare those that break the constitution null and void. In the United States it goes back to Marbury v Madison in 1803, when Chief Justice John Marshall claimed that power for the courts. Lawmakers write the laws; courts check them against the rulebook.

cards.headline: Every court, or one special court?
cards.body: Countries split the job in two ways. In the U.S., any court can hear a claim that a law breaks the constitution. Many European countries, such as Germany and Austria, give that job to a special constitutional court instead. Germany's is the one those 4,640 cases went to.

cards.fact: The UK's Supreme Court can't strike down an Act of Parliament.
cards.context: UK courts must apply Acts of Parliament even if they breach human rights. Higher courts can issue a declaration of incompatibility, but it doesn't change the law or stop it being enforced; Parliament decides whether to fix it. A German court can declare a law void. A UK court can raise a red flag, not show a red card.

title: Police
objective: After this level you can explain what police do and the limits on their power.
summary: London's 1829 police were unarmed and deliberately unmilitary; British policing rests on public consent. The law limits police power: detention time limits, rights in custody, the Miranda warnings.

cards.headline: London's first modern police carried no guns and wore blue on purpose.
cards.body: In 1829 the Metropolitan Police Act, sponsored by Home Secretary Robert Peel, set up a professional police force for London. Its officers carried truncheons, handcuffs and a rattle to call for help. Their blue tailcoats and top hats were chosen to show they were not soldiers. Why work so hard not to look like an army?

cards.headline: Policing by consent
cards.body: Because the idea was to police with the public, not against it. The first of the British policing principles is to prevent crime and disorder, as an alternative to repression by military force. The UK Home Office calls it policing by consent: police power comes from the common consent of the public. In its words, the police are the public and the public are the police.

cards.headline: Powers, with limits
cards.body: Police have real power over people, so the law draws lines. In England and Wales, police can generally hold someone for up to 24 hours before they must charge or release them; longer needs approval for a serious crime. People in custody have the right to free legal advice and to tell someone where they are. In the U.S., Miranda v Arizona (1966) requires police to tell suspects in custody of their right to stay silent and to have a lawyer before questioning.

cards.fact: Only about 4 in 100 police officers in England and Wales are armed.
cards.context: Home Office figures show 6,558 armed officers on 31 March 2026, 4.0% of all police officers. The rest patrol without a gun, nearly two centuries after the first bobbies set out with a truncheon and a rattle.

title: Prisons and Punishment
objective: After this level you can explain the purposes of punishment and the debates about it.
summary: About 11.7 million people were in prison in 2023. Punishment aims at retribution, deterrence, incapacitation or rehabilitation; Kant, Bentham and Beccaria argued over why.

cards.headline: About 11.7 million people were in prison worldwide in 2023.
cards.body: That's the UN Office on Drugs and Crime's count. Around 30 per cent of them, more than 3.7 million people, hadn't been sentenced: they were in pre-trial detention. So what is prison for? Your answer changes what a prison should look like.

cards.headline: Four reasons to punish
cards.body: Four aims come up again and again. Retribution: the offender pays for the wrong done. Deterrence: the threat of punishment discourages crime. Incapacitation: someone locked up can't reoffend outside. Rehabilitation: reform, so the person returns as a law-abiding citizen. A single prison sentence can try to do all four at once, and they don't always pull the same way.

cards.headline: Deserved, or useful?
cards.body: Philosophers split on the deepest question. Retributivists such as Immanuel Kant argue punishment is justified because the wrongdoer deserves it, whatever its effects. Jeremy Bentham took the other side: all punishment is in itself evil, he wrote, justified only as far as it prevents some greater evil. The debate is still going, and it shapes real sentences.

cards.fact: Getting caught matters more than the length of the sentence.
cards.context: That was Cesare Beccaria's argument in On Crimes and Punishments (1764): the certainty of punishment deters more than its severity. A speed camera you know is there changes your driving more than a huge fine you'll probably never get.

cards.headline: Norway's answer
cards.body: Norway's prison service follows a principle of normality: the punishment is the loss of liberty, and no other rights are removed by the sentencing court. Life inside should resemble life outside as much as possible. It's a system built around the rehabilitation aim. Countries weigh the four aims differently, and that's where the debate lives.

title: Checkpoint: Courts and Justice
objective: After this level you can explain how courts, police and punishment fit together.
summary: Justice's symbols sum up the chapter: scales for impartial weighing (courts, juries, the burden of proof), a sword for the power to enforce (police, punishment), and a blindfold for independence.

cards.headline: Look up at London's Old Bailey and Justice is staring straight back.
cards.body: The gilded statue on the dome of England's most famous criminal court holds a sword in one hand and scales in the other. Unlike most statues of Justice, she wears no blindfold. Scales, sword, blindfold: three props. Between them, they sum up this whole chapter.

cards.headline: The scales: weighing the case
cards.body: Justice comes from a Roman virtue, and her scales came to stand for impartiality. That's Level 51's courts, weighing facts against the law. It's Level 53's jurors, weighing the evidence. And it's Level 54's rule for how the scales start: tipped toward the accused, until the prosecution proves guilt beyond reasonable doubt.

cards.headline: The sword: the power to enforce
cards.body: Her sword stands for power. A verdict is only words until someone can enforce it, and that's where Level 58's police and Level 59's punishment come in. But the sword answers to the scales: police work within legal limits, and a sentence follows only a conviction. Power first and weighing later is the order a fair system refuses.

cards.fact: The blindfold arrived in the 16th century.
cards.context: From then on Justice was often shown blindfolded, and today the blindfold is read as a symbol of impartiality: she judges without looking at who stands before her. Level 52's independent judges wear it invisibly.

title: Why Elections?
objective: After this level you can explain what elections are for.
summary: Schumpeter: elections are a contest for votes that picks who rules. Popper: they let the ruled dismiss rulers without bloodshed. UDHR Article 21 bases authority on the will of the people.

cards.headline: Every few years, whole countries can fire their government. Nobody gets hurt.
cards.body: Swapping the people in charge of a country, peacefully and on a schedule, is an odd thing when you stop to think about it. So what exactly are elections for? An economist, a philosopher and the United Nations each gave an answer.

cards.headline: Schumpeter: a contest for your vote
cards.body: In 1942 the economist Joseph Schumpeter gave a blunt answer. Democracy, he wrote, is a method in which people win the power to decide through a "competitive struggle for the people's vote." Citizens don't really rule, in his view: elections are a fairly peaceful way of keeping or changing those who do. Think of a job interview where the whole country sits on the panel.

mascot.line: Popper's test is the one to keep: can today's winners be voted out tomorrow?

cards.headline: Popper: the power to fire
cards.body: The philosopher Karl Popper, author of The Open Society and Its Enemies (1945), shifted the question. "The people do not rule anywhere," he wrote; governments rule. What matters is that the ruled can dismiss their rulers without bloodshed, for example through general elections. For Popper, the test of a democracy isn't who wins. It's whether today's winners can be voted out tomorrow.

cards.headline: The UN: where authority comes from
cards.body: In 1948 the Universal Declaration of Human Rights put a third answer in writing. Article 21 says the will of the people shall be the basis of the authority of government, expressed in periodic and genuine elections. Remember Level 3? Authority is power people accept as legitimate. Elections measure that acceptance again and again instead of assuming it. Locke's consent of the governed, on a timetable.

title: The Secret Ballot
objective: After this level you can explain why voting is secret.
summary: Open voting invited intimidation and bribery. Victoria introduced the modern secret ballot in 1856 and Britain followed in 1872. John Stuart Mill argued voting should be public.

cards.headline: In 1843 New South Wales, you said your vote out loud. Often in a pub.
cards.body: At the New South Wales elections of 1843, voters told an officer, out loud, who they were voting for. Candidates handed out free drinks, and intimidation and bribery were everywhere. The fix came from Australia too.

cards.headline: Victoria's quiet revolution
cards.body: Victoria's secret ballot law took effect on 19 March 1856: the first modern secret ballot. The government printed the ballot papers, not the candidates. You marked yours in private, folded it and dropped it in a box. South Australia soon added a neat tweak: mark an X beside the candidate you want. That version is known as the Australian ballot.

cards.headline: No witness, no threat
cards.body: The logic is simple: if nobody can see your vote, nobody can intimidate you or punish you for it. Britain's Ballot Act of 1872 ended open voting there, a system that had become known for bribery, intimidation and drunken disorder. In 1948 the UDHR from Level 61 wrote secrecy in: elections held by secret vote or equivalent free procedures.

cards.headline: The great dissenter
cards.body: Not everyone cheered. John Stuart Mill, in Considerations on Representative Government (1861), argued that a vote is power over others, so it's a trust held for the public. Like any public duty, he said, it should be done "under the eye and criticism of the public." A secret ballot, he feared, invites people to vote for their own benefit instead.

title: Voting Systems
objective: After this level you can compare winner-take-all and proportional voting.
summary: FPTP elects each district's top vote-getter; PR matches seats to votes; ranked systems transfer preferences. New Zealand moved to MMP. Arrow showed every system trades something.

cards.headline: In 1978, one New Zealand party won the most votes. The other one won power.
cards.body: It happened again in 1981. Both times Labour won more votes nationwide, but National won more seats and kept governing, and criticism of the voting system grew. How can that happen? It depends on how votes turn into seats.

cards.headline: First past the post
cards.body: In first-past-the-post, used in the UK, Canada, India and the United States, each district elects one member: whoever gets the most votes, majority or not. Win lots of districts narrowly and you can take more seats with fewer votes. In the 1950s the political scientist Maurice Duverger observed that this system tends to squeeze politics into two big parties.

cards.headline: Proportional representation
cards.body: Proportional representation aims straight at New Zealand's problem: a party's share of the votes becomes a matching share of seats. Districts elect several members; in Israel and the Netherlands the whole country is one district. New Zealand switched. A Royal Commission recommended Germany's mixed system (MMP) in 1986, and from 1996 voters got two votes: one for a local MP, one for a party.

cards.headline: Ranked choice
cards.body: Ranked systems ask for more than one choice. Australia's House of Representatives uses the Alternative Vote: rank the candidates, and if nobody has a majority, the least successful are eliminated and their votes pass to next preferences until someone does. Ireland's Single Transferable Vote uses rankings in districts that elect several members, keeping results fairly proportional.

title: Drawing the Map
objective: After this level you can explain voting districts and gerrymandering.
summary: District lines can decide results. Canada redraws after each census with independent commissions. Gerrymandering packs and cracks voters; geography alone can also create bias.

cards.headline: Same voters. Same votes. Move the lines, and you change the winner.
cards.body: Picture 100 voters, split 50-50 between two parties, divided into four districts. Draw the lines one way and each party wins two seats. Draw them another way and either party can win three. Nobody changed their vote. Only the map moved.

cards.headline: Why maps get redrawn
cards.body: Level 63's first-past-the-post elects one member per district, so where the lines fall matters. People move, so lines must move too. Canada redraws its federal districts after every 10-year census. Since 1964, independent commissions do the drawing, one per province, each chaired by a judge, and sitting lawmakers can't serve on them.

cards.headline: Meet the gerrymander
cards.body: In 1812, Massachusetts governor Elbridge Gerry signed a bill creating oddly shaped districts that helped his party. A cartoon in the Boston Gazette drew one as a salamander-like monster: the "Gerry-mander." The name stuck. Gerrymandering means deliberately drawing district lines to help or hurt a particular political interest.

mascot.line: Packing and cracking are easy to swap. Packing piles voters up; cracking spreads them thin.

cards.headline: Packing and cracking
cards.body: Two moves do most of the work. Packing crowds a group's voters into as few districts as possible, so they win a few seats by landslides. Cracking spreads them thinly across many districts, so they lose narrowly almost everywhere. Either way, that group ends up with fewer seats than its votes suggest.

cards.headline: Proving it is harder

But Jowei Chen and Jonathan Rodden (2013) found that when one party's voters cluster in cities, even maps drawn without intent can short it seats. Geography can gerrymander by accident.

title: Campaigns
objective: After this level you can explain how election campaigns work.
summary: Lazarsfeld's 1940 study found media changed few votes; people decided through conversations and opinion leaders. The UK caps party spending; Buckley v. Valeo struck down US spending limits.

cards.headline: In 1940, researchers set out to watch a campaign change minds. It mostly didn't.
cards.body: Paul Lazarsfeld and his team interviewed the same voters again and again in Erie County, Ohio, through a US presidential race. Their book, The People's Choice (1944), surprised even its authors, and it changed how people think about campaigns.

cards.headline: Your neighbor beat the radio
cards.body: Contrary to their expectations, the researchers found that radio and newspapers had only minor direct effects on how people voted. People mainly made up their minds by talking with those around them: family, friends, coworkers. The loudest broadcasts of the campaign were outvoted by the kitchen table.

cards.headline: The two-step flow
cards.body: So how do campaign messages travel? Lazarsfeld's answer was the two-step flow. Ideas move from the media to opinion leaders, the people who follow politics closely, and then from them to their followers through personal networks. Much of what you hear from a campaign reaches you secondhand, through someone you trust.

cards.headline: Rules for the race
cards.body: Level 61's Schumpeter called democracy a competitive struggle for the people's vote, and every competition needs rules. The UK caps how much each party may spend in the 365 days before a general election. In the US, the Supreme Court's Buckley v. Valeo (1976) upheld limits on contributions but struck down limits on spending as restricting free expression.

title: Polls
objective: After this level you can explain opinion polls and their margin of error.
summary: The 1936 Literary Digest poll's 2.4 million biased replies lost to Gallup's scientific sample. A plus or minus 3 margin needs about 1,067 random interviews; a lead's margin is about double.

cards.headline: In 1936, 2.4 million people answered a magazine's poll. It still got it wrong.
cards.body: The Literary Digest mailed about 10 million straw ballots, got 2.4 million back and predicted Alf Landon would beat Franklin Roosevelt. Roosevelt won easily. How can so many answers be so wrong?

cards.headline: Big isn't the same as fair
cards.body: The Digest drew its names from phone lists, car registrations and club memberships. During the Depression, those leaned heavily toward the well-off, and only about a quarter of those mailed replied. George Gallup used more systematic, scientific sampling and publicly predicted that Roosevelt would win handily. A poll is only as good as who's in it.

cards.headline: The margin of error
cards.body: A well-chosen sample works like a spoonful from a well-stirred pot of soup. A simple random sample of 1,067 people has a margin of error of about plus or minus 3 points. That means if you ran the same survey 100 times, the result would land within 3 points of the true value about 95 times.

mascot.line: If you keep one habit from this level, make it this: check the margin on the lead before you believe it.

cards.headline: Read the lead, not just the number
cards.body: Here's the trap. The margin on the gap between two candidates is roughly double: a 3-point margin becomes about 6 points for the lead. So a 5-point lead could really be anywhere from -1 to +11. And sampling is only one source of error; question wording and who answers matter too.

title: Referendums
objective: After this level you can explain direct votes on a single question.
summary: A referendum puts one question to voters; an initiative starts with a citizens' petition. New Zealand chose MMP by referendum in 1993. Bulmer weighs benefits and risks; questions must be clear.

cards.headline: In 1988, Chile's ruler called a vote to keep himself in power. He lost.
cards.body: Augusto Pinochet, Chile's authoritarian ruler, held a referendum to extend his term. He unexpectedly lost, and his regime collapsed shortly after. One yes-or-no question turned out to be very powerful. So who gets to ask it?

cards.headline: One question, straight to the voters
cards.body: A referendum gives people a direct vote on a specific issue, sent to them by a parliament, president or government. A citizens' initiative works the other way round: the people start it, usually with a petition signed by a set number of people. Results can be binding or only advisory, though advisory votes are usually treated as binding in practice, especially if decisive.

cards.headline: Voters choose the rules
cards.body: Remember Level 63's New Zealand? It settled its voting-system argument by asking the voters. In a binding referendum in 1993, 53.9% chose MMP over first-past-the-post. The people chose the method that would count their own votes.

cards.headline: Worth it? The debate
cards.body: Elliot Bulmer's primer for International IDEA weighs both sides. For: you vote on one measure on its merits, not a party's whole package. Against: voters may react to unrelated things, like how popular the leaders are; frequent votes cause fatigue; rulers can use referendums to fake legitimacy. The Venice Commission adds a rule: the question must be clear, not misleading, and must not suggest an answer.

title: Counting the Votes
objective: After this level you can explain how votes are counted and checked.
summary: UK counts are watched by candidates' agents, recounts can be requested and ties go to lots. India's VVPAT slips and Philip Stark's risk-limiting audits let counts be checked.

cards.headline: In a UK election, an exact tie is settled by drawing lots.
cards.body: If two candidates tie and one more vote would decide it, the returning officer must decide between them by lot. But that only happens after every ballot has been counted, and checked, with witnesses watching. This level is about the witnesses.

cards.headline: Counting in the open
cards.body: At UK elections, each candidate can appoint counting agents to watch the verification and the count, and the process is meant to be transparent. If an agent doubts the result, they can ask for a recount. The returning officer must consider it, can refuse only an unreasonable request, and any recount happens in full view of everyone there.

cards.headline: A paper trail for machines
cards.body: Machines count fast, but can you check them? In India, a VVPAT printer beside each voting machine shows the voter a paper slip with their candidate's name and symbol for 7 seconds. Then it drops into a sealed box. Those slips can be counted, so the machine's tally has something to answer to.

cards.headline: Checking without recounting everything
cards.body: In 2007 the statistician Philip Stark developed the risk-limiting audit. Officials hand-check randomly chosen paper ballots. If the sample doesn't confirm the result, the audit grows, up to a full hand count that replaces the reported result. It has been tested in California, Ohio and Denmark. As Stark puts it, "unlike voters, ballots have to reply, and have to reply truthfully."

title: Spotting Misinformation
objective: After this level you can spot misleading claims about politics.
summary: Misinformation, disinformation and malinformation differ by truth and intent. Fact checkers read laterally. Caulfield's SIFT: Stop, Investigate the source, Find better coverage, Trace.

cards.headline: Who judges a website best: a historian, a Stanford student or a fact checker?
cards.body: Sam Wineburg and Sarah McGrew put 10 PhD historians, 10 professional fact checkers and 25 Stanford undergraduates in front of live websites on social and political issues. One group was far better and faster. Its trick works on any election claim you'll ever meet.

cards.headline: Three kinds of bad information
cards.body: First, some words. In a 2017 report for the Council of Europe, Claire Wardle and Hossein Derakhshan separated three things. Misinformation is false but shared without meaning harm. Disinformation is false and shared knowingly to cause harm. Malinformation is genuine, but shared to cause harm. Same shape, different intent.

mascot.line: Read sideways. If you take one habit from this level, take that one.

cards.headline: Read sideways
cards.body: The historians and students often fell for official-looking logos and domain names. They read vertically, staying on a site to judge it. The fact checkers read laterally: after a quick scan, they left the site and opened new tabs to see what others said about it. They reached better-founded conclusions in a fraction of the time. Don't ask a website whether it's trustworthy. Ask everyone else.

cards.headline: SIFT before you share
cards.body: Mike Caulfield turned this into four moves, SIFT. Stop: when you hit a post, ask whether you know the source before reading or sharing. Investigate the source. Find better coverage. Trace claims, quotes and media back to their original context, because much of what we see online has been stripped of it, like a clip that leaves out what happened just before.

title: Checkpoint: Elections

summary: The IPU's 1994 Declaration on free and fair elections lists this chapter's ideas: authority from the people, a secret and equal vote, fair campaigns and an honest, observed count.

cards.headline: In 1994, the Inter-Parliamentary Union wrote a checklist for fair elections.
cards.body: On 26 March 1994 in Paris, the Inter-Parliamentary Council unanimously adopted the IPU's Declaration on Criteria for Free and Fair Elections. Read it now and it looks like this chapter's table of contents.

cards.headline: From a ballot to power
cards.body: Follow one vote through this chapter. It's cast in secret, turned into seats by a voting system and a district map, fought over in a campaign and counted in the open. What comes out is Level 3's authority: power people accept as legitimate. And Popper's point makes it complete: the ruled can dismiss their rulers without bloodshed, so next time the same vote can take that power away.

title: Government Budgets
objective: After this level you can explain how a government plans its spending.
summary: A budget, once a leather bag, is a government's plan for what it collects and spends. It runs through four overlapping stages: prepare, approve, carry out and audit.

cards.headline: In 1733, a pamphlet mocked Britain's top minister for opening his bag.
cards.body: The pamphlet was called The Budget Opened, and it attacked Robert Walpole's tax plans, likening him to a quack selling cures. The insult stuck. By the 1760s, 'budget' was simply the word for a government's money plans.

cards.headline: A plan in a bag
cards.body: The word comes from Old French bougette, a small leather bag: picture a finance minister opening his wallet to reveal his plans. Britain's chancellor still holds up a red box on Budget Day. Inside is a plan with two sides: the money the government expects to collect, much of it Level 6's compulsory taxes, and the money it intends to spend over the coming year.

mascot.line: Hold on to these four stages; later levels in this chapter keep coming back to them.

title: Where Tax Money Goes
objective: After this level you can describe what governments spend the most on.
summary: OECD governments spent 42.6% of GDP in 2023. The biggest slice is social protection (pensions and benefits), then health; the size of that slice varies widely between countries.

cards.headline: If government spending were a pizza, which slice would be biggest?
cards.body: Defence? Schools? Roads? Take a guess before you scroll. In every EU country the answer is the same, and it's none of those.

cards.headline: First, the size of the pizza
cards.body: Across OECD countries, government spending averaged 42.6% of GDP in 2023. That's measured against GDP, the value of everything an economy produces in a year. Some countries go well past it: in 2024 Finland, France and Austria each spent more than half. Level 6's taxes, about a third of GDP, pay for much of it.

cards.headline: Ten standard slices
cards.body: To compare countries fairly, statisticians cut spending into ten standard functions, known as COFOG: general public services, defence, public order and safety, economic affairs, health, education, social protection and a few smaller ones. Social protection is the one nobody guesses. It covers pensions, plus benefits for people who are sick, disabled or out of work.

mascot.line: If you remember one thing here: the biggest slice is social protection, not defence or schools.

cards.fact: The biggest slice is social protection: 13.4% of GDP across the OECD in 2023.

title: Public Schools
objective: After this level you can explain how public schools are run and paid for.
summary: Who runs a school and who pays for it are separate questions. Dutch private schools get equal state funding; countries also differ in which level of government pays.

cards.headline: Who runs your school, and who pays for it? The answers needn't match.
cards.body: In the Netherlands, the state funds public schools and private schools equally. The private ones are usually run by foundations based on a religion or other beliefs. So a Dutch school can be private and still paid for by taxes.

cards.headline: Run by whom, paid by whom
cards.body: The OECD sorts schools by who controls them. Public schools are typically funded and regulated by government. Private schools are run by a private body, and they come in two kinds. Government-dependent private schools get more than half their money from public sources; independent ones live mainly on fees and donations. Dutch private schools are almost all the first kind.

cards.fact: OECD governments spend about 2.2% of GDP on primary and lower secondary schools.
cards.context: That's the 2022 average; Iceland spent the most, 3.2%. Rich doesn't automatically mean a bigger share. Luxembourg spends among the most per pupil, yet less than the average share of GDP, because its GDP per person is among the highest.

cards.headline: Which level of government pays?
cards.body: Remember Level 8's layers? For upper secondary schools, Greece, Iceland and New Zealand fund everything from the centre. In Spain, the regions provide and manage over 80% of the public money; in Switzerland, the cantons spend 94%. It's the same idea as Level 8's Canada, where the provinces run education. Same school corridors, very different paymasters.

title: Healthcare Systems
objective: After this level you can compare the main ways countries pay for healthcare.
summary: Countries pay for healthcare through tax-funded government schemes, compulsory insurance or out of pocket, in different mixes. The US spent 17.2% of GDP on health in 2024; the OECD average, 9.3%.

cards.headline: Every country pays its doctors. The question is whose pocket pays.
cards.body: Nobody gets healthcare for free: nurses, scanners and medicines all cost money. What differs from country to country is the route the money takes, and the OECD sorts those routes into a few big pipes.

items.label: Government schemes

items.label: Out of pocket

mascot.line: No system is free. The question to keep is who writes the cheque, and how.

cards.headline: Pipes, not boxes
cards.body: Most countries mix the pipes rather than pick one. In a government scheme, you're covered because you live there, and the bill goes to the taxpayer. In compulsory insurance, you're covered because contributions are paid for you, usually by you and your employer together. Neither is free; they differ in who writes the cheque and how. Out-of-pocket payments are the leftover, and in some countries it's a big leftover.

cards.context: The OECD average was 9.3%, and Germany came next at 12.3%. Across the OECD, health also took 15.1% of all government spending in 2023. Which system works best is argued fiercely. The WHO's stated goal for all of them is universal health coverage: the care people need, when they need it, without financial hardship.

title: Pensions
objective: After this level you can explain how pensions support older people.
summary: Public pensions cost OECD countries 8.1% of GDP, about 18% of government spending. More older people per worker is pushing retirement ages up, as in Denmark's move to 70.

cards.headline: The world's first state pension started at 70. Denmark is heading back there.
cards.body: Germany's 1889 scheme set the pension age at 70, and lowered it to 65 in 1916. In May 2025, Denmark's parliament confirmed its pension age will reach 70 from 2040, the highest in Europe. Why would a country turn the clock back more than a century?

cards.fact: Public pensions cost OECD countries 8.1% of GDP on average.
cards.context: That's up from 6.7% in 2000, and it's about 18% of all government spending. Pensions are a big part of Level 72's biggest slice, social protection. The range is wide: Greece and Italy spend around 16% of GDP, Iceland and Ireland under 3%. In Iceland, as in Australia, compulsory workplace schemes carry much of the load.

cards.headline: More grandparents per worker
cards.body: Here's the squeeze. Across the OECD, there were 22 people aged 65 or over for every 100 aged 20 to 64 in 2000. By 2025 there were 33, and the projection for 2050 is 52. The OECD treats this ratio as a stand-in for potential pensioners per potential contributor. Each step up means fewer shoulders under each pension.

cards.headline: Working longer, and arguing about it
cards.body: One response is a later retirement age. Under laws already passed, the OECD's average normal retirement age for men will rise from 64.7 to 66.4 for people starting work in 2024. Denmark shows both sides of the debate. Its government said the rise was needed to afford proper welfare for future generations; unions protested it as unjust.

title: Roads and Bridges
objective: After this level you can explain how governments build and maintain infrastructure.
summary: Genoa's bridge collapse showed that infrastructure must be maintained. Governments pay for roads with taxes, road-user taxes like the US fuel tax, or public-private partnerships.

cards.headline: On 14 August 2018, a motorway bridge in Genoa fell.
cards.body: The Morandi bridge had carried traffic since 1967. When it collapsed, 43 people died. A bridge is built once, but it has to be looked after for as long as it stands.

cards.fact: Genoa's new bridge came with its own robots.
cards.context: The San Giorgio bridge, designed by Renzo Piano, opened in August 2020. Four robots run along it, checking for weathering and erosion. It's maintenance built into the design: the dull, never-finished job that decides whether infrastructure lasts.

cards.headline: Who pays? Often, the drivers
cards.body: In 1956 the United States set up the Highway Trust Fund to help build the Interstate highways, paid for by taxes on road users, such as fuel taxes. The people who use the roads pay at the pump. The catch: the federal gas tax has been 18.4 cents a gallon since 1993, and since the late 2000s Congress has had to top the fund up repeatedly.

cards.headline: Or bring in a partner
cards.body: Another route is a public-private partnership, or PPP. In the OECD's definition, it's a long-term deal in which a private company funds and delivers a public service, like a road, and shares the risks. The European Court of Auditors agreed in 2018 that PPPs can speed delivery and keep up maintenance. But when it checked 12 EU-backed PPPs, seven of nine finished projects ran late, by up to 52 months.

title: Corruption
objective: After this level you can explain corruption and how countries fight it.
summary: Corruption is the abuse of entrusted power for private gain. Hong Kong's ICAC, set up in 1974, fought it with enforcement, prevention and education; Transparency International measures perceptions.

cards.headline: In early-1970s Hong Kong, you might have to bribe an ambulance crew.
cards.body: Crews asked for 'tea money' before picking up a sick person. Bribes smoothed the way to public housing and school places too. A public service came with a private price tag.

mascot.line: Entrusted, abuse, private gain: keep all three words and you have the definition.

cards.headline: Borrowed power, misused
cards.body: Transparency International defines corruption as the abuse of entrusted power for private gain. Every word matters. Entrusted: the power was lent to an official by the public. Abuse: it was used for something it wasn't lent for. Private gain: the official pockets the benefit. Remember Level 3? Authority is power people accept. Corruption quietly turns it into a price list.

cards.fact: The ICAC fought corruption three ways: enforcement, prevention and education.
cards.context: Catch the corrupt, fix the systems that tempt them, and bring the public on side. It also stood apart from any government department, because corruption was worst in the police force itself. You can't ask the suspects to run the investigation.

cards.fact: Denmark tops the 2025 Corruption Perceptions Index, with 89 out of 100.
cards.context: Transparency International scores 182 countries and territories on perceived public-sector corruption, from 0 (highly corrupt) to 100 (very clean). In 2025 the global average fell to 42, and 122 countries scored below 50. It was Denmark's eighth year in a row at the top.

title: Deficits and Debt
objective: After this level you can explain government deficits and debt.
summary: A deficit is spending above revenue in a year; borrowing to cover deficits builds debt. The IMF expects global public debt to pass 100% of GDP by 2029. Views on limits differ.

cards.headline: Global public debt is heading for its highest level since 1948.
cards.body: That's the IMF's projection: government debt worldwide rising above 100% of world GDP by 2029. How does a government end up owing more than a year's worth of everything its economy produces? One year at a time.

cards.headline: The yearly gap
cards.body: Level 71's budget has two sides. When spending beats revenue, the gap is a deficit; the reverse is a surplus. To cover a deficit, a government borrows, mostly by selling bonds: 79.3% of OECD public debt takes that form. Run deficits year after year and they pile up as debt.

cards.fact: In 2023, only six OECD countries ran a surplus.
cards.context: The average OECD government ran a deficit of 4.6% of GDP. Norway led the small surplus club at 16.5%.

mascot.line: Owing a lot isn't the same as being in trouble. A debt's size isn't the whole story; its cost matters too.

cards.headline: Big debts, different risks
cards.body: Among the G20, Canada, China, France, Italy, Japan, the UK and the US have debts above 100% of GDP, or soon will. The IMF rates their risk as moderate, thanks to deep markets for their bonds. Meanwhile 55 countries are in or near debt distress, often with debts below 60%. The size of a debt isn't the whole story; its cost matters too.

title: The Military
objective: After this level you can explain what militaries do and who controls them.
summary: Militaries carry the state's force for defence, under the control of elected civilians and parliaments. The world spent $2887 billion on them in 2025; how much is enough is debated.

cards.headline: Costa Rica has had no army since 1949.
cards.body: Its constitution abolishes the army as a permanent institution, and keeps the police forces needed for public order. UNESCO notes the money went into social development, especially health and education. So what are armies for, and who decides what they do?

cards.headline: The state's force, with a leash
cards.body: Remember Level 9's Weber? A state claims the monopoly of legitimate force within its territory. The military is the heaviest part of that force, and it provides Level 5's classic public good, national defence. That makes one question vital: who holds the leash?

cards.headline: Civilians in charge
cards.body: In a democracy, the armed forces answer to democratically elected authorities, overseen by the courts, the media and civil society. Civilians decide the military's missions, size, budget and purchases; commanders decide how to carry the missions out. Parliaments add laws, hearings and control of the purse, so Level 71's approval stage applies to tanks too.

cards.fact: The world spent $2887 billion on the military in 2025.
cards.context: That's SIPRI's count, equal to 2.5% of global GDP and 6.9% of the average government's spending. The five biggest spenders, the United States, China, Russia, Germany and India, made up 58% of it.

cards.headline: How much is enough?
cards.body: Every country answers for itself, and NATO's members answered together. In 2014 they aimed for 2% of GDP by 2024; in June 2025 they agreed on 5% by 2035, at least 3.5% of it for core defence. SIPRI, which tracks the spending, warns the looser part of the target could invite 'creative accounting', with non-military projects relabelled as defence.

title: Checkpoint: Money and Government
objective: After this level you can explain how governments raise and spend money.
summary: Every budget ends with an audit. Independent auditors, backed by the 1977 Lima Declaration, check public money. Chapter 8: raise, plan, spend, check.

cards.headline: Every budget ends the same way: someone checks the receipts.
cards.body: Level 71's cycle had a fourth stage, audit, where the actual spending is checked. This chapter followed the money from taxes to pensions, bridges and tanks. This level follows the people who follow the money.

cards.headline: Auditors who answer to no minister
cards.body: Countries' top auditors are called supreme audit institutions. In 1977 they adopted the Lima Declaration, known as the Magna Carta of government auditing, and its chief aim is independent auditing. Level 76's European Court of Auditors shows the job: it asked not only 'was the money spent?' but 'did it deliver?', and found PPPs running up to 52 months late.

cards.headline: Follow one euro
cards.body: Try it with a single euro of tax. It arrives on the collecting side of Level 71's budget. The biggest share of spending goes on social protection, so it may well end up in someone's pension. If the government spent more than it collected, some of what it spent was borrowed. And after the year ends, an auditor checks that the money went where the budget said.

title: Sovereignty
objective: After this level you can explain what makes a country independent.
summary: Sovereignty is a state's final say over its own affairs. Westphalia (1648) is seen as the start of the state system; Montevideo (1933) lists four tests for a state.

cards.headline: On 9 July 2011, the world gained a brand-new country.
cards.body: South Sudan became independent that day, the newest country on Earth, and five days later the UN admitted it as a member state. Remember Level 1's 193 UN members? South Sudan is the newest of them. So what exactly did it gain that day? In one word: sovereignty.

cards.headline: The final say
cards.body: Britannica defines sovereignty as the ultimate power or authority in a state's decision-making and in keeping order. Put simply, a sovereign state has the final say over its own affairs: which laws apply, who runs things, how order is kept. It's the difference between owning your house and renting a room in someone else's.

cards.fact: Modern sovereignty is often traced to a peace deal of 1648.
cards.context: The Peace of Westphalia, negotiated in the German towns of Munster and Osnabruck, ended the Thirty Years' War. It recognized the full territorial sovereignty of the empire's member states, including the right to make their own treaties. Many scholars see it as the foundation of the modern system of independent, equal states: lots of separate houses instead of one landlord.

cards.headline: A four-point checklist
cards.body: How do you recognize a state? The Montevideo Convention, signed in 1933, lists four qualifications: a permanent population, a defined territory, a government, and the capacity to enter into relations with other states. Level 9's state already had territory and laws; the fourth test looks outward. And Article 3 adds a twist: a state's existence doesn't depend on other states recognizing it.

title: Diplomacy
objective: After this level you can explain how ambassadors and diplomats work.
summary: Embassies represent, protect, negotiate and report. The 1961 Vienna Convention makes embassies inviolable and diplomats immune, but the host can send any diplomat home.

cards.headline: Police can go almost anywhere in a city. An embassy's door stops them.
cards.body: Under the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations, an embassy's premises are inviolable: the host country's officials may not enter without the consent of the head of the mission. Why would a sovereign country accept a door it can't open on its own soil?

cards.headline: What an embassy is for
cards.body: An embassy is one country's permanent office inside another. The Vienna Convention lists its jobs: represent its country, protect its interests and citizens, negotiate with the host government, report home on what's happening, and promote friendly relations. None of it is forced: diplomatic relations are set up by mutual consent. Level 81's fourth test for a state was the capacity to enter into relations with other states. Embassies are that capacity at work.

cards.fact: Protecting envoys is an ancient rule, written down in 1961.
cards.context: The Vienna Convention's preamble recalls that peoples of all nations from ancient times have recognized the status of diplomats. The Convention itself, signed on 18 April 1961, wrote down rules that had been stable for over 200 years, and almost all states are now parties. Diplomacy's rulebook was mostly copied out, not invented.

mascot.line: Immunity isn't a license to misbehave. It protects the mission's work, not the person.

cards.headline: Can't arrest you, can send you home
cards.body: A diplomat can't be arrested or detained, and is immune from the host country's criminal courts. That sounds like a license to misbehave, but the Convention says immunity isn't there to benefit individuals: it lets missions do their work without coercion or harassment. Diplomats must still respect local laws. And the host holds a trump card: it can declare any diplomat persona non grata, at any time, without saying why, and the sending country must recall them.

title: Treaties
objective: After this level you can explain how countries make treaties.
summary: A treaty is a written agreement between states. Signing comes first; ratification binds. Then pacta sunt servanda: agreements must be kept.

cards.headline: A copy of the oldest known peace treaty hangs at the UN.
cards.body: Around 1269 BC, the Hittite king Hattusili III and Egypt's Ramesses II put peace in writing. They pledged lasting peace, nonaggression, extradition and mutual help. A replica now hangs near the entrance of the Security Council Chamber at UN Headquarters. Countries still make their biggest promises the same way: in writing.

cards.headline: Whatever you call it
cards.body: Pact, convention, protocol, agreement: the label doesn't matter. The Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties (1969) defines a treaty as a written agreement between states, governed by international law, whatever its particular name. Working out the words is diplomats' work: negotiating with the host government was one of Level 82's embassy jobs. Think of a treaty as a contract, with countries as the signatures.

mascot.line: Signing and ratifying are easy to mix up. When a treaty needs both, only ratification binds.

cards.headline: Sign first, bind later
cards.body: Signing is often not the last step. When a treaty needs ratification, a signature doesn't bind the state yet; ratification is the act by which a state consents to be bound. In between, a signer must not do anything that would defeat the treaty's purpose, unless it makes clear it won't join. The pen says "we mean to"; ratification says "we will".

cards.fact: Pacta sunt servanda: agreements must be kept.
cards.context: That Latin phrase is arguably the oldest principle of international law. The 1969 Vienna Convention puts it in Article 26: every treaty in force binds its parties and must be performed in good faith. Article 27 closes the obvious loophole: a country can't point to its own laws as an excuse for failing to keep a treaty.

title: The United Nations
objective: After this level you can explain what the UN does and does not do.
summary: Founded in 1945 to prevent war, the UN gives every member one vote in the General Assembly; the Security Council's five permanent members hold a veto. It is not a world government.

cards.headline: The UN's founding document opens with a promise about war.
cards.body: Its first words set the mission: "to save succeeding generations from the scourge of war, which twice in our lifetime has brought untold sorrow to mankind." Everything the UN does, and everything it can't do, makes more sense once you know it began with that sentence.

cards.headline: Signed in San Francisco
cards.body: Delegates from 50 countries spent two months in San Francisco in 1945 drawing up the UN Charter. The UN came into existence on 24 October 1945, once China, France, the Soviet Union, the UK, the US and most other signers had ratified it. Ratified: Level 83's step, the one that turns a signature into a binding promise.

cards.headline: One country, one vote
cards.body: In the General Assembly, all 193 members sit together and each has one vote, so Tuvalu's vote counts exactly as much as India's. The Charter calls this the sovereign equality of all its members: Level 81's idea, written into the rules. The Assembly makes recommendations to states, and important questions need a two-thirds majority.

cards.headline: Fifteen seats, five vetoes
cards.body: Keeping the peace is mainly the Security Council's job. It has 15 members, 5 of them permanent: China, France, Russia, the UK and the US. Unlike the Assembly's recommendations, its decisions bind every UN member. A decision needs nine votes, including all five permanent members, so a single no from any one of them blocks it. That's the veto.

cards.fact: The UN is not a world government.
cards.context: In its own words, the UN is neither a supra-state nor a government of governments. It has no army and levies no taxes, and it depends on what its member states are willing to do. Back to Level 1's ship: the UN isn't a captain for every vessel. It's where the captains meet.

title: The European Union
objective: After this level you can explain how the EU works.
summary: The EU began with six countries pooling coal and steel to make war impossible. Today 27 members share lawmaking: the Commission proposes; Parliament and Council adopt.

cards.headline: It started with coal, steel and a plan to make war impossible.
cards.body: On 9 May 1950, French foreign minister Robert Schuman proposed pooling Western Europe's coal and steel industries. His aim was to make war between France and Germany "not merely unthinkable, but materially impossible." Today's European Union grew from that idea.

cards.fact: Six countries went first, in 1951.
cards.context: Belgium, France, Germany, Italy, Luxembourg and the Netherlands signed a treaty to run their coal and steel industries jointly, so no single country could make the weapons of war to turn against the others. The goal was to end the bloody conflicts that had culminated in the Second World War. That first step led to today's European Union of 27 countries.

cards.headline: Laws made in a triangle
cards.body: Everything the EU does rests on treaties its member countries agreed to voluntarily and democratically. Lawmaking runs through a triangle. The European Commission proposes a law. Two bodies adopt it: the European Parliament, directly elected by EU citizens, and the Council of the EU, where ministers from each member government sit. The member countries then put it into practice, and the Commission checks that they do.

cards.headline: Sharing the final say
cards.body: Remember Level 81: sovereignty means having the final say. EU members agreed, by treaty, to make some of their laws together, through a Parliament and a Council they all share, instead of each deciding alone. The final say hasn't vanished: in treaties they chose to sign, the members agreed to share some of it.

title: War and Peace
objective: After this level you can explain how wars start and how they end.
summary: Clausewitz saw war as politics by other means. Rules on starting wars tightened from 1907 to 1945. An armistice stops a war; a peace treaty ends it.

cards.headline: On 11 November 1918, the guns fell silent. The war wasn't over yet.
cards.body: That day's armistice stopped the fighting on the Western Front, but the First World War formally ended only with the Treaty of Versailles, signed on 28 June 1919. Stopping a war and ending one turn out to be different steps. So is starting one.

cards.headline: Politics by other means
cards.body: Why do wars start? One classic answer comes from the Prussian general Carl von Clausewitz, whose book On War appeared in 1832, after his death. He argued that war is a continuation of state policy by other means. In his view, war isn't a break from politics: it's a tool governments pick up to pursue political goals.

title: International Courts
objective: After this level you can explain courts that judge countries and war crimes.
summary: Nuremberg held that people commit crimes against international law. The ICJ settles disputes between consenting states; the ICC tries individuals as a court of last resort.

cards.headline: In 1946, a court ruled that crimes are committed by people, not abstractions.
cards.body: The International Military Tribunal at Nuremberg, run by the US, UK, Soviet Union and France, tried 22 leading Nazi officials. Its judgment put it plainly: "Crimes against international law are committed by men, not by abstract entities." A state can't stand in the dock. The people who act in its name can.

cards.headline: Two courts, one city
cards.body: The Hague in the Netherlands hosts two very different international courts. The first is the International Court of Justice, which sits in the Peace Palace. It's the UN's principal judicial organ, and the only one of the UN's six main organs not based in New York. Its 15 judges are elected for nine-year terms by the General Assembly and the Security Council, Level 84's two big bodies.

cards.headline: Countries versus countries
cards.body: Only states can be parties in cases at the ICJ. And a state can't simply be dragged in: the Court's jurisdiction rests on the consent of the states involved. So the ICJ is where countries bring legal disputes with each other, and it also gives advisory opinions when UN bodies ask for one. Think of it as a court for arguments between sovereigns.

mascot.line: ICJ: country against country. ICC: a person in the dock. One letter apart, worlds apart.

cards.headline: People in the dock
cards.body: The second court, the International Criminal Court, works the other way round: it tries individuals. Set up by a treaty called the Rome Statute, it deals with genocide, war crimes, crimes against humanity and the crime of aggression committed since 1 July 2002. It's a court of last resort, meant to complement national courts, not replace them. Nuremberg set the precedent that people answer for such crimes.

title: Refugees
objective: After this level you can explain refugees and the right to asylum.
summary: Nansen's 1922 passport helped refugees with no country. The 1951 Convention defines refugees and forbids returning them to danger. Most displaced people stay inside their country.

cards.headline: In 1922, a polar explorer created a passport for people with no country.
cards.body: In 1921 the League of Nations made Fridtjof Nansen its first High Commissioner for Refugees, to help people fleeing Russia after the revolution. Many had lost their nationality. His "Nansen passport" let them travel to other countries to look for work; about 450,000 people used one. Nansen received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1922.

cards.headline: Who counts as a refugee
cards.body: Today's rule comes from the 1951 Refugee Convention. A refugee is someone outside their own country who can't or won't return to its protection because of a well-founded fear of being persecuted for their race, religion, nationality, membership of a particular social group or political opinion. And UNHCR says refugee status is declaratory: you're a refugee from the moment you meet the criteria, before any official says so.

cards.fact: The core rule: no sending refugees back into danger.
cards.context: It's called non-refoulement. Article 33 of the 1951 Convention says a refugee must not be expelled or returned to a territory where their life or freedom would be threatened, and UNHCR calls it one of the most fundamental principles of international law. Asylum is the protection a state grants to someone fleeing persecution or serious harm, and UNHCR says seeking it is a human right.

cards.fact: Most people forced from home never cross a border.

title: Problems Without Borders
objective: After this level you can explain problems no country can solve alone, like climate change.
summary: Ozone and climate cross every border, and countries are tempted to free ride. The Montreal Protocol was ratified by all; under Paris each country sets its own plan.

cards.headline: One treaty has been ratified by every country. It's about the sky.
cards.body: The Montreal Protocol, signed in 1987, set out to phase out the chemicals that were depleting the ozone layer. It became the first treaty in UN history to be ratified by every country. Why would a treaty about chemicals need the whole world on board?

cards.headline: Problems that ignore passports
cards.body: Some problems don't stop at the border. The UN calls climate change a global emergency that goes beyond national borders and needs international cooperation. As an OpenStax economics textbook puts it, no nation by itself can cut greenhouse gas emissions enough to solve global warming without the cooperation of other nations. The atmosphere has no customs checkpoint.

mascot.line: This is Level 5's free rider again, now wearing a flag.

cards.headline: Free riders, planet-sized
cards.body: Remember Level 5's free riders, who enjoy a public good while letting others pay? cards.body: On 1 December 1959, twelve countries whose scientists had taken part in the International Geophysical Year (1957–58) signed the Antarctic Treaty in Washington. It came into force in 1961 and now has 58 parties. It's this chapter in a single document.

cards.headline: Sovereignty, parked

cards.headline: Peace, science and open doors
cards.body: Article I says Antarctica shall be used for peaceful purposes only: no military bases, no nuclear explosions. Scientists keep the freedom to investigate and must share their results. title: Citizenship
objective: After this level you can explain what citizenship means.
summary: Citizenship is a two-way bond with a state: allegiance for protection. Most people get it at birth by soil (jus soli) or blood (jus sanguinis); adults can naturalize.

cards.headline: You probably never applied for your first citizenship.

cards.headline: A two-way deal
cards.body: Britannica defines citizenship as the relationship between an individual and a state to which the individual owes allegiance and in turn is entitled to its protection. Read that as a trade. You owe the state loyalty; the state owes you protection. Remember Level 9's state, with its territory, laws and means of enforcing them? Citizenship is your membership card for one.

title: Rights and Responsibilities
objective: After this level you can explain the duties that come with rights.
summary: Rights come with responsibilities. Some are legal duties, like obeying the law and jury service when called; others are civic. Australia turned voting into a legal duty in 1924.

cards.headline: In Australia, skipping an election can land you a penalty.
cards.body: Since 1924, voting at Australian federal elections has been a legal duty, not just a right. Miss it without a valid and sufficient reason and you face a penalty. That raises a bigger question: what do citizens owe in return for their rights?

cards.headline: Rights come with responsibilities
cards.body: Canada's official citizenship guide puts it in one line: in Canada, rights come with responsibilities. It's an old idea. Level 7's social contract set out the rights and duties of each side, and Level 91's citizenship trades allegiance for protection. You don't just hold rights. You help keep up the system that protects them.

cards.headline: Must, and should
cards.body: The guide's list includes obeying the law, serving on a jury, voting in elections, helping others in your community, and protecting heritage and the environment. Some are enforced by law. If you're called for jury duty, the guide says, you are legally required to serve. Level 6's taxes belong with the musts too: they're compulsory. Voting is on the list as well. Whether the law makes you do it depends on the country.

cards.fact: Australia's turnout jumped from under 60% to over 91%.
cards.context: In 1922, fewer than 60% of eligible Australians voted in the federal election. Voting became compulsory in 1924, and at the 1925 election turnout rose to over 91%. Same country, same kind of election, one change to the rule. Whether voting should be a legal must or a civic should is a choice each country makes for itself.

title: Speaking to Your Representative
objective: After this level you can explain how to contact elected officials.
summary: A UK MP represents everyone in the constituency, voters or not. Write with your address, visit a surgery, or sign a petition: 10,000 signatures earn a UK government reply, 100,000 a debate.

cards.headline: Your representative works for you, even if you voted for someone else.
cards.body: Take the UK. MPs are elected to represent the interests and concerns of all the people who live in their constituency, whether they voted for them or not. So the job includes you. The question is how to get their attention.

cards.headline: Step one: find your person
cards.body: In the UK, each MP represents one area, called a constituency, and can normally only take up issues raised by the people who live there, their constituents. So start with your address. Find out who represents it, then put that address in your letter or email. It tells the office you're one of theirs, not a stranger from across the country.

cards.headline: Step two: go and talk
cards.body: Most MPs also hold surgeries in their constituency: sessions where you can meet them and talk through a problem. Remember Level 3's legal-rational authority, which belongs to the office and not the person? That's why this works. You're not begging a favor from a stranger. You're using an office that exists partly to hear you.

cards.context: UK Parliament petitions get a government response at 10,000 signatures and are considered for debate at 100,000. Canada's House of Commons sets a lower bar: an e-petition with at least 500 signatures is presented, and the government responds within 45 days. One letter speaks for you. A petition speaks for a crowd.

title: Volunteering
