summary: Volunteering is unpaid, non-compulsory work, formal or informal. About 862 million people volunteer monthly, and some public services, like NSW's fire brigades, run largely on volunteers.

cards.headline: One Australian state's fire service runs on about 70,000 volunteers.
cards.body: The NSW Rural Fire Service in New South Wales has about 70,000 volunteer members and is widely described as the largest volunteer fire service in the world. Fire protection is on Level 5's list of public services. Here, a huge force of unpaid people helps provide it.

mascot.line: Keep this contrast: taxes are what everyone must give, volunteering what people choose to give.

cards.headline: Unpaid, and unforced
cards.body: The International Labour Organization defines volunteer work as unpaid, non-compulsory work: time people give without pay, either through an organization or directly for others outside their own household. Compare Level 6's taxes, which are compulsory. Taxes are what everyone must give. Volunteering is what people choose to give.

cards.headline: Mostly without a uniform
cards.body: Formal volunteering happens through an organization, like a fire brigade. Informal volunteering is arranged directly between people: shopping for a sick neighbor, fixing a friend's fence. Worldwide, more than twice as many people volunteer informally as formally. So most volunteering happens without any roster or badge at all.

cards.context: That's the estimate in UN Volunteers' 2022 State of the World's Volunteerism Report, counting people aged 15 and over. By definition, nobody is made to give that time, and nobody is paid for it. It's a workforce no budget pays for.

title: Reading the News Well
objective: After this level you can judge whether a news story is reliable.
summary: Many shared links are never read. Journalists' own codes give readers clues: headlines backed by the text, clearly identified sources, labeled opinion, and prompt corrections.

cards.headline: In one study, most shared news links were never even clicked.
cards.body: In 2016, researchers at Columbia University and France's Inria found that 59% of the news links shared on Twitter in their sample were never clicked. Plenty of headlines travel without their stories. So how do you judge the story itself? Journalists' own rulebooks offer clues.

cards.headline: Clue 1: the headline isn't the story
cards.body: The UK's Editors' Code, enforced by the press regulator IPSO, tells the press not to publish misleading information, including headlines not supported by the text. That rule exists because the problem does. A headline is a pitch, written short. Read far enough to see whether the story actually backs it up.

cards.headline: Clue 2: who says so?
cards.body: The US Society of Professional Journalists' Code of Ethics tells reporters to identify sources clearly, so the public can judge how reliable they are and why they're talking. A trustworthy story shows its workings: named people, documents, data. If you can't tell how the reporter knows something, you can't check it either.

cards.headline: Clue 3: news or opinion?
cards.body: Both codes draw the same line. The SPJ says to label advocacy and commentary. The UK code says the press, while free to campaign, must distinguish clearly between comment, conjecture and fact. Opinion isn't a flaw; it's a different product. Check the label before you treat an argument as a report.

cards.fact: A correction is a good sign, not a bad one.
cards.context: The SPJ tells journalists to correct mistakes promptly and prominently. The UK code says significant inaccuracies must be corrected promptly and with due prominence. An outlet that runs corrections is showing you it checks its own work.

title: Young People and Politics
objective: After this level you can describe ways young people take part before they can vote.
summary: The UN Convention on the Rights of the Child gives children a right to be heard. Youth parliaments, letters to representatives and volunteering are ways in before voting age.

cards.headline: In 2009, teenagers took over the green benches of the House of Commons.
cards.body: On 30 October 2009, about 300 Members of the UK Youth Parliament debated in the Commons chamber. It was the first time a group other than MPs had used it. So what can you do in politics before you're old enough to vote?

cards.headline: A right to be heard
cards.body: The UN Convention on the Rights of the Child, adopted in 1989, is the world's most widely ratified human rights treaty. It counts everyone under 18 as a child, unless the law sets adulthood earlier. Its Article 12 gives a child capable of forming views the right to express them freely in all matters affecting them, given due weight for age and maturity. Too young to vote isn't too young to be heard.

cards.headline: Practice parliaments
cards.body: Youth parliaments turn that right into a habit. In the UK Youth Parliament, any young person aged 11 to 18 can vote or stand, members are elected, and once elected they run campaigns on issues that matter to young people. It's the real machinery in miniature. You learn politics the way you learn to swim: by getting in.

cards.headline: Tools that don't need a ballot

title: Local Government Up Close
objective: After this level you can describe how a city or town council works.
summary: Cities use designs like council-manager and mayor-council. English council meetings are public, agendas out five clear days ahead; India's gram sabha includes every village voter.

cards.headline: In an Indian village, every voter belongs to the local assembly.
cards.body: India's gram sabha is made up of everyone on the village panchayat's electoral roll, and it approves development plans before the panchayat carries them out. Remember Level 8's panchayats? This is the room they answer to. A big city can't fit every voter in one room, though. So how does an elected council run one?

cards.headline: Open doors, published papers
cards.body: In England, the Local Government Act 1972 says a council meeting is open to the public, except when the public is lawfully kept out, for example for confidential matters. The agenda and reports must be open for inspection at least five clear days before. So you can read what's coming, then walk in and watch it being decided.

cards.body: So what will you actually hear about? Level 8's list for Canada's municipal governments is a good guide: fire protection, local police, public transit, parks, waste management, water supply and local roads. National politics gets the headlines. Your council decides whether the bins get emptied on time.

title: Myths About Government
objective: After this level you can debunk common myths about how government works.
summary: Three myths checked against the rules: a higher tax bracket taxes only the income inside it; UK civil servants serve any elected government; MPs represent everyone in their area.

cards.headline: Get a raise, jump a tax bracket, take home less. Sound right?
cards.body: You may have heard it. It's wrong, at least for income tax in the US and the UK. This level checks three common beliefs about government against the actual rules.

mascot.line: People get this one backwards. Only the income above the line pays the higher rate.

cards.headline: Myth 1: a higher bracket taxes everything
cards.body: Income taxes in the US and the UK use brackets (the UK calls them bands). Each rate applies only to the part of your income inside its bracket. Cross into a higher one and only the income above the line pays the higher rate. Everything below is taxed exactly as before. Your earlier dollars and pounds never notice.

cards.headline: Myth 2: new government, new staff
cards.body: When a new party takes power, does it bring in its own officials? In the UK, the civil service is built on the opposite idea. Its code requires civil servants to serve the government, whatever its political persuasion, and to serve different governments equally well. They must not let their own political views decide their advice. The politicians at the top change; the code expects the staff to serve whoever wins.

cards.headline: Myth 3: your representative only works for their voters
cards.body: Level 93 already busted this one. UK MPs are elected to represent everyone who lives in their constituency, whether they voted for them or not. Winning an election puts someone in an office, and Level 3's legal-rational authority belongs to the office, not to its fan club.

learned: A higher bracket taxes only the income inside it

title: How to Disagree Well
objective: After this level you can argue about politics without falling out.
summary: Mill: know the other side at its strongest. Dennett's Rapoport rules: restate, agree, credit, then criticize. Graham: aim at the central point, not the person.

cards.headline: "He who knows only his own side of the case, knows little of that."
cards.body: John Stuart Mill wrote that in On Liberty, in 1859. It's a bold claim: being sure you're right isn't the same as knowing why. This level is about arguing with people you disagree with, and still being on speaking terms afterwards.

cards.headline: Know their best case
cards.body: Mill's reasoning: if you can't answer the other side's reasons, or don't even know them, you have no ground for preferring either opinion. And he wanted those reasons heard from people who actually believe them, in their most plausible and persuasive form. A cartoon of your opponent is easy to beat. It's also not who you're arguing with.

cards.headline: Four steps before the rebuttal
cards.body: Philosopher Daniel Dennett, drawing on game theorist Anatol Rapoport, gave a recipe in 2013. First, restate the other view so well its holder says, "Thanks, I wish I'd thought of putting it that way." Second, list where you agree. Third, mention anything you learned from them. Only then, criticize. By step four, they're actually listening.

mascot.line: If you keep one thing from this level: argue with the point, not the person.

cards.headline: Aim high on the ladder
cards.body: Paul Graham's 2008 essay How to Disagree ranks replies from worst to best. At the bottom: name-calling, then ad hominem (attacking the person), then responding to tone. At the top: refuting the central point. Low rungs are about the person. High rungs are about the argument.

cards.headline: Political animals, still
cards.body: Level 10's Aristotle said humans are by nature political animals: we live in communities, so we're bound to disagree inside them. The aim isn't a world without arguments. It's arguments that leave the community standing.
